clips.title: Poland is $55 away from passing Spain (IMF, Oct 2026) #Shorts
clips.desc: 2008: Spain $34.4k vs Poland $19.7k per person (PPP). 2026: $60,106 vs $60,051. IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026.

clips.title: Spain gained 3 million people. Poland lost 1.7 million #Shorts
clips.desc: Both have about 1.1 births per woman. The difference is immigration (World Bank WDI).

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, PPP (current international $); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: In 2008, the average Spaniard produced about thirty-four thousand dollars a year, adjusted for prices. The average Pole, less than twenty thousand. {p} Spain was almost seventy-five percent richer. {pp} This year, according to the IMF's newest numbers, the gap is fifty-five dollars. {p} Not fifty-five percent. Fifty-five dollars, per person, per year. {p} About sixty thousand one hundred for Spain. About sixty thousand and fifty for Poland. {p} That's less than a tenth of one percent.

In February, Poland's prime minister, Donald Tusk, said Poland had already passed Spain in income per person. In Spain, newspapers called it el sorpasso. {p} But the numbers he quoted were older forecasts. The IMF's October update says: not yet. Spain is still ahead, by a hair. {pp} And the same forecast has Poland passing Spain next year, in 2027, and pulling about seven percent ahead by 2030.

So how did a country that spent the 1980s under communism catch one of Western Europe's big four economies? {p} And if the two are basically tied, why does Spain still feel so much richer when you visit? {pp} <soft>It's a story about a crash, a long run, and a population puzzle.</soft>

shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP per capita, PPP (constant 2021 international $), change since 2008 · European Stability Mechanism: financial assistance to Spain's banking sector, 2012–2013 (up to €100 billion; €41.3 billion disbursed)
shots.narration: Spain's trouble started with bricks. {p} In the 2000s, its economy ran on a housing boom fueled by cheap credit. At the peak, construction employed more than one Spanish worker in eight. When the bubble burst in 2008, it took banks and millions of jobs down with it. {p} In 2012, Spain needed a European rescue for its banks: up to a hundred billion euros of credit, of which it used about forty-one. {pp} After inflation, output per Spaniard fell about nine percent from 2008 to 2013. {p} It didn't get back to its 2008 level until 2017. {p} Then the pandemic knocked it down again: in 2020, Spain's economy shrank by about eleven percent, the worst fall in the European Union.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · unemployment, total and youth (% of labor force, modeled ILO estimate)
shots.narration: And the jobs went with it. {p} In 2013, about twenty-six percent of Spaniards who wanted work couldn't find it. Among young people, more than half. {p} Poland's unemployment that year was about ten percent. {pp} Today, Poland has one of the lowest unemployment rates in Europe: about three percent. {p} Spain's has fallen a long way, to just over ten percent. But that's still the highest in the European Union. And almost one in four young Spaniards is still out of work.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP growth (annual %), 1992–2025; GDP per capita, PPP (constant 2021 international $)
shots.title: Poland's long run
shots.narration: Poland, meanwhile, just kept growing. {p} Since 1992, its economy has shrunk in exactly one year: 2020, the pandemic. {p} In 2009, the worst year of the global financial crisis, Poland was the only economy in the European Union that grew. {pp} After inflation, output per Pole has risen about eighty-four percent since 2008. Spain's, about ten percent. {p} No housing bubble on Spain's scale, no bank rescue, and a lot of investment. Poland has been the biggest recipient of EU development money: motorways, railways, factories. {p} And unlike Spain, Poland never joined the euro. When the crisis hit, the złoty fell, Polish exports got cheaper, and the economy kept moving.

shots.src: Eurostat earn_mw_cur · monthly minimum wage (EUR), January; Spain's 14 yearly payments spread over 12 months
shots.narration: You can see it in paychecks. {p} In 2008, Spain's minimum wage was about seven hundred euros a month. Poland's, about three hundred and forty. {p} By 2025, Spain's had risen to about thirteen hundred and eighty, after a push of about sixty percent since 2018. Poland's, to about eleven hundred. {pp} So Spain's is still higher. But Poland's has more than tripled, while Spain's almost doubled. {p} And things cost less in Poland, so a Polish minimum wage goes further than the euro figure suggests.

Quick favor: if you're enjoying this, hit subscribe. One country passing another, with the real numbers, every day. {p} Now, the part most comparisons miss: the people. Who is actually sharing the pie?

shots.src: World Bank WDI · population, total; fertility rate (births per woman) · IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita PPP × population
shots.narration: A number per person has two halves: the economy on top, and the people underneath. {p} Since 2008, Spain's population has grown by more than three million, about seven percent. Poland's has shrunk by about one point seven million, more than four percent. {p} The odd part: both have some of the lowest birth rates in Europe, about one point one children per woman. {p} The difference is immigration. Spain draws newcomers by the million, many from Latin America, who already speak the language and can apply for citizenship after just two years. Today, about one in five people living in Spain was born abroad. {p} Many young Poles, after 2004, went west instead. {pp} So Spain's economy stretches over more people, and Poland's is shared by fewer. {p} Measured as a whole economy, adjusted for prices, Spain is still more than a third bigger. {p} The per-person race is close. The size race isn't.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · life expectancy at birth, total (years), 2024
shots.title: Life expectancy, 2024
shots.narration: But here's the twist: on almost everything you can feel, Spain is still ahead. {p} Spaniards live about eighty-four years on average. {pp} Poles, about seventy-eight and a half. That's five and a half more years of life.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, current US$ (NGDPDPC), 2026 · Eurostat prc_ppp_ind · GDP per capita in PPS (EU27 = 100), 2024
shots.title: Other measuring sticks
shots.narration: In plain dollars, without adjusting for prices, the IMF puts Spain about a third ahead this year: almost forty-two thousand dollars per person, against about thirty-one thousand. {p} And Europe's own statistics office, Eurostat, measures prices differently. On its numbers, Spain is still clearly ahead: about ninety-two percent of the EU average in 2024, against Poland's seventy-nine. {pp} The IMF and Eurostat are both right. They just use different price surveys. {p} And part of why Spain feels rich is that you see it at its best: almost ninety-seven million foreign tourists visited in 2025, a record. About two for every Spaniard.

So what does Poland actually win? {p} Growth: last year, about three point seven percent, against two point six for Spain. {p} Jobs: unemployment less than a third of Spain's. {p} And debt: Spain's government owes about a hundred percent of its economy. Poland's, about sixty. {pp} Though Poland's debt is rising fast: last year it ran one of the biggest budget deficits in the EU, about seven percent.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, PPP (current international $); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: So what happens next? {p} By the IMF's numbers, Poland passes Japan this year, and Spain should follow in 2027. {p} By 2030, Poland would be about seven percent ahead of Spain, about six percent ahead of Japan, and within about two and a half percent of Italy. {pp} But forecasts are not facts. This one has already moved once: the numbers Tusk quoted had Poland ahead. {p} And Poland's growth is expected to slow, to about two and a half percent a year, as its population shrinks.

labels.at: two and a half percent of Italy

shots.narration: So, has Poland passed Spain? {p} Adjusted for prices, not yet: it's fifty-five dollars short. In plain dollars, Spain is still about a third ahead. In life expectancy, five and a half years. {p} But in 2008, Spain was almost seventy-five percent richer. That gap has closed to almost nothing in eighteen years. The real test is next year, when the IMF has Poland in front. {pp} <soft>Which country do you think Poland passes after Spain?</soft> Tell me in the comments.
Spain isn't the first big name on the list. This year, by the same numbers, Poland passed Japan. To see how, watch this next. {p} I'm Chartbound. See you in the next one.

yt.title: Poland Is $55 Away From Passing Spain
yt.description:
In 2008 the average Spaniard produced almost 75% more than the average Pole, adjusted for prices. In the IMF's October 2026 World Economic Outlook, the gap this year is $55 per person: $60,106 for Spain, $60,051 for Poland. The same forecast has Poland ahead in 2027. Spain's lost decade, Poland's long run, the population puzzle, and why Spain is still ahead in dollars, wages and life expectancy.

Sources: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 (PPPPC, NGDPDPC, NGDP_RPCH, LUR, LP); World Bank WDI (NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD, NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG, SL.UEM.TOTL.ZS, SL.UEM.1524.ZS, SP.POP.TOTL, SP.DYN.TFRT.IN, SP.DYN.LE00.IN); Eurostat (prc_ppp_ind, earn_mw_cur, gov_10dd_edpt1); European Stability Mechanism (Spain, 2012–2013); Polskie Radio and Euronews (Feb 2026).
{music_credits}
